article.description: Una galaxia barrada de gran tamaño ocupa el centro de la escena en esta imagen del 22 de octubre de 2026, pero el lente gravitacional en la esquina inferior derecha es el verdadero objetivo. Esta observación es una de las muchas imágenes de lente gravitacional tomadas por el Telescopio Espacial Hubble de la NASA en preparación para la ciencia con el nuevo Telescopio Espacial Nancy Grace Roman. Los astrónomos utilizarán estos […]
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: El Hubble de la NASA marca el camino para el telescopio espacial Roman**

El telescopio espacial Hubble de la NASA ha capturado imágenes que servirán como base para las futuras observaciones del telescopio Nancy Grace Roman, programado para su lanzamiento en 2027. En una imagen reciente, tomada el 22 de octubre de 2026, se observa una galaxia espiral con un lente gravitacional en la esquina inferior derecha, lo que permite a los astrónomos estudiar las distorsiones gravitacionales y su relación con la materia oscura.

Estas imágenes son parte de una serie de observaciones que Hubble ha realizado para preparar el terreno para el Roman, que se enfocará en investigar la estructura del universo y la naturaleza de la materia oscura. Los científicos esperan que la colaboración entre ambos telescopios proporcione una visión más completa del cosmos, permitiendo avances significativos en la comprensión de fenómenos astronómicos.

El telescopio Roman, con su capacidad para observar grandes áreas del cielo, complementará las observaciones detalladas de Hubble, ofreciendo nuevas oportunidades para explorar el universo y responder preguntas fundamentales sobre su composición y evolución.
article.original_title: NASA’s Hubble Marks Way for Roman Space Telescope
article.source_body: A sinuous spiral galaxy (center) appears in the same field of view as a vivid gravitational lens (right corner) in this Hubble image. NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) A sweeping barred galaxy takes center stage in this Oct. 22, 2026, image, but the gravitational lensing at bottom right is the real target. This observation is one of many gravitational lensing images taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for science with the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope . Astronomers will use these images to analyze gravitational distortions to learn more about dark matter in the foreground galaxies and to lay the groundwork for future Roman observations. Images like this offer a glimpse of how Hubble and Roman will work together to build an even more comprehensive picture of the cosmos. Image credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America)

article.description: Investigadores del Instituto Smithsonian revelan que la Luna se está encogiendo: detectan más de 10 mil fallas tectónicas Enséñame de Ciencia -
article.explanation:
Investigadores del Instituto Smithsonian han realizado un hallazgo significativo sobre la Luna, revelando que este satélite natural se está encogiendo. Este fenómeno ha llevado a la detección de más de 10 mil fallas tectónicas en su superficie. 

El encogimiento de la Luna se debe a procesos geológicos que han estado ocurriendo a lo largo de millones de años. A medida que el interior lunar se enfría, la corteza se contrae, lo que provoca la formación de estas fallas. Las fallas tectónicas son fracturas en la superficie donde se ha producido un desplazamiento, y su gran número indica que la Luna ha experimentado cambios significativos en su estructura.

Este descubrimiento no solo proporciona información sobre la historia geológica de la Luna, sino que también ayuda a los científicos a comprender mejor los procesos que han dado forma a otros cuerpos celestes en nuestro sistema solar. La investigación sobre estas fallas puede ofrecer pistas sobre la actividad tectónica y la evolución de la Luna a lo largo del tiempo.
article.title: Investigadores del Instituto Smithsonian revelan que la Luna se está encogiendo: detectan más de 10 mil fallas tectónicas

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: NASA Nombra a Troy Asher Director del Centro de Investigación de Vuelo Armstrong**

NASA ha designado a Troy Asher como el nuevo director del Armstrong Flight Research Center, ubicado en Edwards, California. Asher, un experimentado piloto de pruebas e ingeniero aeroespacial, había estado desempeñando el cargo de director interino desde marzo de este año. Jared Isaacman, administrador de NASA, destacó que Asher ha dedicado su carrera a expandir los límites del vuelo, tanto como piloto de aeronaves experimentales como líder de equipos en misiones complejas.

El Armstrong Flight Research Center es fundamental para la reconstrucción del portafolio de aviones X de NASA y para el avance de la investigación en vuelo. Asher supervisará las operaciones y el personal del centro, que juega un papel crucial en el desarrollo de nuevas tecnologías de aviación y en la realización de misiones científicas aéreas.

Antes de asumir el cargo de director interino, Asher fue director de Operaciones de Vuelo en Armstrong, donde gestionó a pilotos, ingenieros y una flota de aeronaves especializadas. Su trayectoria incluye una carrera de 24 años en la Fuerza Aérea de EE. UU., donde estableció 25 récords mundiales de velocidad volando el bombardero B-1B. Con su nombramiento, se espera que Asher impulse la innovación en la investigación aeroespacial y fortalezca las capacidades de NASA en este campo.
article.original_title: NASA Names Troy Asher Armstrong Flight Research Center Director
article.source_body: Photo of Troy Asher NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Troy Asher director of the agency’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Asher, a veteran test pilot and aerospace engineer with decades of experience in flight research and operations, has served as the center’s acting director since March. “Troy has spent his career pushing the boundaries of flight, both at the controls of experimental aircraft and leading the teams that make these missions possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “He understands what it takes to turn ambitious ideas into successful flight tests, and his experience will be invaluable as Armstrong leads the way in rebuilding NASA’s X-plane portfolio, restoring our flight-test capabilities, and flying higher, farther, and faster than we have in decades.” “Flight testing demands a rare combination of technical excellence, operational judgment, and trust in the teams that make every mission possible,” said NASA Associate Administrator and Chief Engineer Amit Kshatriya. “Troy’s service to America, from his distinguished career as an Air Force test pilot to his leadership of some of NASA’s most challenging flight research missions, embodies those qualities. Few people better understand the art and discipline of flight testing, and he brings a deep understanding of both the aircraft and the teams behind every successful mission. As director, Troy will help us revolutionize how we develop, evaluate, and fly new technologies, strengthening the capabilities that keep NASA at the forefront of aerospace research.” Asher will oversee Armstrong’s workforce and operations, leading NASA’s efforts to advance flight research, aircraft operations, and the development of new aviation technologies. As NASA’s Flight Test and Aircraft Operations Center of Excellence, Armstrong plays a central role in the agency’s efforts to rebuild and expand its X-plane portfolio, pushing the boundaries of high-speed flight and developing experimental aircraft and technologies that will shape the future of aviation. The center also supports airborne science missions and flight research across the agency. Prior to becoming acting center director, Asher served as director of Flight Operations at Armstrong, overseeing the center’s pilots, engineers, maintainers, and fleet of specialized aircraft supporting aeronautics research and scientific missions around the world. Asher joined NASA in 2008 as a research test pilot and aerospace engineer. During his time as a NASA pilot, he conducted flight research aboard aircraft, including the F-15, F/A-18, Gulfstream III, and X-56A unmanned aircraft system. He served as the lead test pilot for the development of NASA’s Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy (SOFIA) and flew scientific research missions aboard the agency’s DC-8 aircraft, supporting airborne science campaigns around the globe. Before joining NASA, Asher completed a 24-year career in the U.S. Air Force, retiring as a lieutenant colonel. His military service included assignments as an instructor at the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School at Edwards Air Force Base, commander of the 419th Flight Test Squadron, and director of the Bomber Combined Test Force. In 2003, he set 25 world speed records flying the B-1B bomber. Asher earned a bachelor’s degree in astronautical engineering from the U.S. Air Force Academy and a master’s degree in mechanical engineering from California State University, Fresno. Asher succeeds Bradley Flick, who retired in March following nearly 40 years of NASA service. Established in 1946, Armstrong has been at the forefront of American flight research for eight decades, from the first supersonic flight aboard the Bell X-1 to today’s work advancing quiet supersonic flight through NASA’s X-59 aircraft. The center continues to push the boundaries of aviation while providing critical flight research and operational capabilities in support of NASA’s science, technology, and exploration missions. article.explanation:
**TITULAR: El Desafío Universitario de la NASA Enciende la Trayectoria de un Emprendedor de Drones**

Gavin Gardner, un joven emprendedor de Michigan, ha transformado su experiencia en el Desafío Universitario de la NASA en una exitosa carrera en el desarrollo de drones. En 2024, junto a su hermano Gryson y otros exalumnos del programa, fundó AG3 Labs, una empresa dedicada a la fabricación de drones para ejercicios de entrenamiento militar.

Gardner, quien fue estudiante de ingeniería en la Universidad Estatal de Michigan, participó en el programa de la NASA que otorga subvenciones a equipos de estudiantes universitarios. Su primer proyecto, Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), buscaba innovar en la entrega de carga mediante drones que se acoplaran a autobuses urbanos. Aunque el equipo decidió no comercializar esta idea debido a las estrictas regulaciones, su trabajo les valió un segundo premio en 2023 para desarrollar el sistema Laser Energized Aerial Drone System (LEADS).

La experiencia adquirida en el Desafío Universitario no solo les proporcionó habilidades técnicas, sino también conocimientos en gestión empresarial, lo que ha sido crucial para el crecimiento de AG3 Labs. Actualmente, la compañía produce miles de drones al mes, consolidándose como un actor importante en el sector de la tecnología de defensa.
article.original_title: NASA University Challenge Ignites Trajectory of Drone Entrepreneur
article.source_body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Four co-founders of AG3 Labs –from left Matt Atkinson, Gavin Gardner, Ryan Atkinson, and Gryson Gardner – show off the military training drones their company builds at a U.S. Army event at Camp Grayling in Michigan. As a student, Gavin was on a Michigan State team twice selected for participation in NASA’s University Student Research Challenge. His NASA experience served as a foundation for the creation of AG3. AG3 Labs Five years ago, Gavin Gardner was a Michigan State University engineering student researching next-generation drone technology as part of a NASA grant. Garder expected the research to be demanding – but he was surprised that navigating the financial side of the work presented an even greater challenge. Although Gardner was used to leading fellow students in a lab setting, he and his team were completely new to things like creating budgets, handling large sums of money, and promoting their work for crowdfunding. That’s why demonstrating both engineering and entrepreneurship skills are major tentpoles of NASA’s University Student Research Challenge (USRC), an initiative that provides grants to teams of college students interested in helping the agency realize its aeronautical research goals. “Half the battle is building your product,” Gardner said recently. “The other half is selling the product in a way that everyone else can understand what you’re doing and not talking in nerdy, engineering ways.” We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers. STEVEN HOLZ NASA USRC Manager Gardner and his Michigan State USRC alumni teammates are still using those lessons today, as aerospace developers. In 2024, they founded their own company, AG3 Labs, which specializes in drones for military training exercises. “I don’t think I would discredit our technical expertise in getting us to where we are today, but I know that USRC was a booster that really amplified our trajectory at such a young age,” Gardner said. NASA USRC manager Steven Holz said Gardner’s experience shows what students can accomplish when they receive both a grant and guidance – enabling a future workforce and contributing to the aviation industry. “We are proud to see the success of USRC alumni,” Holz said. “We hope that every team that participates in the program sees, like Gavin, how they can grow technically, entrepreneurially, and use the opportunity as a launchpad for their own innovative careers.” Research path Gardner’s path to running his own company began with a middle school age trip to Space Camp, where he began realizing that he wanted to be an engineer. The engineering bug also bit his brother, Gryson Gardner, and the two of them would often be found in their Michigan garage tinkering with various machinery, including drones and electronic kits. When Gardner arrived at Michigan State, he looked for extracurricular groups and found one dedicated to the increasingly popular hobby of drones. He gained hands-on, practical experience in how drones are made and operated. In 2021, Gardner received an email from a friend who told him they had just won a USRC grant from NASA for an activity called Aerial Intra-city Delivery Electric Drones (AIDED), and they needed help building a new drone. “We had this idea that instead of flying through the whole city, why can’t a drone just hitchhike a ride on a city bus like everyone else does?” Gardner said. The concept was for a cargo-carrying drone to take off, dock on top of public transportation such as a bus, charge its batteries while riding along, and then take off for its final leg of the delivery. The team built and flew a full-scale drone to prove the concept but decided against pursuing a commercial venture. “The commercial drone market kind of scared us a little bit with the large number of regulations that go into operating such a novel idea like this with flying over people in a dense city,” Gardner said. But the team’s demonstration of technical prowess and confidence led to a second USRC award from NASA in 2023 – the Laser Energized Aerial Drone System (LEADS), which focused on using a laser to transfer power directly to a drone in flight. While working on LEADS, which led to flying a prototype, Gardner’s network of contacts within the drone community expanded to include NASA personnel at the Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, who made him aware of internship opportunities, which he applied for and was accepted while in graduate school. Gavin Gardner, a University Student Research Challenge participant who went on to co-found his own drone company, also was a NASA intern in 2024 and wrote this social media post. Student challenge paves way for opportunity As his graduation in the spring of 2025 with a master’s degree approached, Gardner took the initial steps in late 2024 to co-found with his brother and other USRC alumni AG3 Labs after a friend suggested the military could use low-cost drones to test effective counter drone systems. An initial award from the U.S. Army led to more contracts, allowing the company to expand and ramp up its operations, where today their production capability enables thousands of drones to be built each month. Gardner credits his experience with USRC, especially when it came to learning more about the business side of running a technical operation, with helping create the opportunities for success he and his team are experiencing today. About the Author Jim Banke Aeronautics Senior Writer Jim Banke is a veteran aviation and aerospace communicator with more than 40 years of experience as a writer, producer, consultant, and project manager based at Cape Canaveral, Florida. He is part of NASA Aeronautics' Strategic Communications Team and is Senior Writer for the Aeronautics Division within the Research Technology Mission Directorate. In 2007 he was recognized with a Distinguished Public Service Medal, NASA's highest honor for a non-government employee. article.explanation:
**TITULAR: NASA selecciona 19 nuevas propuestas de ciencia ciudadana en 2026**

En un avance significativo para la ciencia colaborativa, la NASA ha seleccionado 19 nuevas propuestas de ciencia ciudadana en 2026, reafirmando su compromiso con la investigación accesible y participativa. Este anuncio se enmarca dentro del programa de financiamiento de semillas para la ciencia ciudadana, que busca involucrar a voluntarios en proyectos científicos innovadores.

Entre los proyectos destacados se encuentra "The Rogue Worlds Project", liderado por Jacqueline Faherty del Museo Americano de Historia Natural, que invita a los participantes a buscar planetas libres en datos de la misión SPHEREx. Otro proyecto, "Planet Hunters Roman", dirigido por Bernard Gaudi de la Universidad Estatal de Ohio, se centra en la detección de exoplanetas a través de la lente de la nueva telescopía espacial Nancy Grace Roman.

Además, el programa incluye iniciativas en heliophysics y ciencias planetarias, como "Space Weather UnderGround", que permitirá a los ciudadanos monitorear la magnetosfera terrestre mediante magnetómetros. Estas propuestas no solo amplían el alcance de la investigación científica, sino que también fomentan la participación activa de la comunidad en la exploración del cosmos.
article.original_title: NASA Selects 19 New Citizen Science Proposals in 2026
article.source_body: Explore This Section Science Citizen Science NASA Selects 19 New Citizen… Overview Resources Opportunities Citizen Science Highlights About Science Activation So far, 2026 has seen a flood of successes for volunteers who do NASA science, exemplifying NASA’s commitment to gold-standard science—transparent, reproducible and intrinsically collaborative. The Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project announced that their project volunteers have now discovered most of the known brown dwarfs , celestial objects that are similar to planets. The Zooniverse platform, with grant from NASA, reached a milestone of 1 billion classifications. Several projects have come online that leverage new super intelligence (SI) techniques to amplify or extend the work of volunteers. More NASA volunteers are using SI to build their own data tools and help write scientific papers than ever before. Even with all of those achievements, our science community is already working on the next round of new volunteer projects and innovations. NASA’s Science Mission Directorate has selected nineteen proposals from research teams in 2026 that will result in new opportunities for you to do NASA science. The Citizen Science Seed Funding Program The Citizen Science Seed Funding Program (CSSFP-25) of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate aims to support scientists and other experts to develop citizen science projects and expand the pool of professional scientists who use citizen science techniques in their science investigations. Twelve new proposals to this program were selected. Astrophysics “The Rogue Worlds Project: Activating volunteers to uncover the hidden population of super Jupiters with SPHEREx” led by Principal Investigator Jacqueline Faherty from the American Museum of Natural History. This project will invite you to search data from NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) mission to find free-floating planets and brown dwarfs in clusters of young stars. The SPHEREx space observatory mapping the entire sky in near-infrared wavelengths. “ Quantifying the calibrations between intrinsic galaxy merger timescales with visual pair/tidal-feature classifications” led by Principal Investigator Kameswara Bharadwaj Mantha of the University of Missouri. This project will investigate galaxy mergers, helping astronomers understand how galaxies evolve through time. You will be invited to classify realistic mock images of galaxies to help probe the statistics and dynamical evolution of galaxy mergers. “ Overlap Zoo; cosmic light tables for galaxy transparency” led by Principal Investigator Benne Holwerda of the University of Louisville. Galaxies, which glow with the light of the billions of stars they contain, also contain dust. This dust is easiest to see and quantify when it overlaps, or is backlit by, another galaxy. Help spot and characterize these rare overlapping galaxy pairs to help reveal how much dust they contain. Overlap Zoo is live! Follow this link to learn more and join the project. “ Planet Hunters Roman: Extending Citizen Science to Planetary Microlensing” led by Principal Investigator Bernard Gaudi of the Ohio State University. Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars other than our Sun. Their gravity can bend the light that travels around them. This project will invite you to spot exoplanets in data from NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope data by the way they bend starlight. Heliophysics “Space Weather UnderGround: Deploying a low-cost Magnetometer Array with Citizens for Heliophysics Research” led by Principal Investigator Hyunju Connor at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. Along with sunshine, our Sun produces the solar wind, an unrelenting flow of charged particles. Earth’s protective magnetic field shield deflects most of these particles, but not all, and not during extreme events. Help scientists monitor the subtle disturbances of Earth’s magnetosphere by the solar wind by setting up and monitoring your own magnetometer in Alaska. “A Citizen Science Initiative for Sonified Plasma Wave Characterization” led by Principal Investigator Lauren Blum of the University Of Colorado, Boulder. “Plasma” is the name given to the ionized gases at the edge of Earth’s magnetosphere. Solar wind, the rain of charged particles that flows out from the Sun, can interact with and generate waves in the plasma. This project will turn data from this dynamic zone into sound signals. You will be invited to listen in to identify waves in the Earth’s magnetosphere. “Revealing the Consequences of Foreshock Transients for Earth’s Magnetospheric System Through Participatory Science” led by Principal Investigator Wenli Mo at the Johns Hopkins University. This project will invite you to examine data from NASA’s MMS (Magnetospheric Multiscale) mission to identify “foreshock transients,” phenomena that have a critical but poorly understood role in space weather. The resulting dataset will help reveal how foreshock transients form, their properties, and their impacts. “IMPACT: Interactive Magnetospheric Particle Analysis and Citizen Technology” led by Principal Investigator Muhammad Fraz Bashir at the University of California, Los Angeles. Energetic particles rain down from the magnetosphere into the upper ionosphere, heating and perturbing the ionosphere, disrupting the scatter of radio waves and GPS operations. This project will invite you to help match patterns between two types of data: measurements from satellites flying overhead that detect energetic particles raining down from space and measurements from ground-based instruments that detect electromagnetic waves. By comparing these patterns, volunteers will help scientists figure out which types of space waves are causing different kinds of particle precipitation, and in turn, help scientists better understand and predict disruptions to GPS and increased radiation risks during space weather events. “Unlocking Clues About Particle Acceleration and Transport Using Particle Distributions” led by Principal Investigator Gang Kai Poh at the Catholic University Of America. NASA’s Advanced Composition Explorer, Parker Solar Probe, and Solar Orbiter are complementary missions gathering data to help scientists improve understanding of the Sun, solar wind, and space weather. Examine data from these missions to contribute to the study of the complicated flow of energetic particles from the Sun. “Data Fusion in Space: Combining Citizen Observations to Classify Solar Wind Tracers” led by Principal Investigator Cynthia Lopez-Portela of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County. This project will invite you to use their pattern-recognition skills to spot features in images of the Sun’s corona, where the solar wind begins. These features can be used as tracers to help scientists track the movement of the solar wind and build better models of how it behaves. Planetary Sciences “Mapping Lunar Iron Abundance Hotspots to Enable In-Situ Resource Utilization of Regolith Consolidation Technologies” led by Principal Investigator Karen Martirosyan at the University of Texas, Rio Grande Valley. Building a base on the Moon will require creative use of Moon materials. So what materials will future teams of astronaut base-builders have to work with? This project will invite you to help locate iron deposits in data from NASA’s Moon Mineralogy Mapper mission to help understand how the Moon formed and to aid future exploration. “Small Body Discovery and Outburst Monitoring with a Worldwide Citizen Science Telescope Network” led by Principal Investigator Ariel Graykowski at the SETI Institute. This project proposes to activate a global network of citizen scientists, each equipped with a standardized small-aperture telescope, to conduct follow-up observation of cometary outbursts and small moving bodies (comets, near-Earth asteroids, and main-belt asteroids). With their global distribution and a program of twilight observations, amateurs will complement professional surveys. The project will develop systems to automate processing of contributed images and to distribute alerts for objects of interest to the network. The Science Activation Program The Science Activation Program (SciAct) from NASA’s Science Mission Directorate supports a portfolio of competitively selected, collaborative project teams that extend the impact of NASA science. These “SciAct Teams” accomplish this by connecting people and communities – many of whom would not otherwise meaningfully engage – with NASA science data and experts, local partnerships, and authentic science experiences. Seven teams selected in the latest round of competition will engage learners with citizen science efforts directly related to NASA research priorities. Several other selected teams plan to incorporate citizen science projects or community science projects (research efforts led by and focused on specific communities) into their work. The selected proposals include: “Growing Beyond Earth: Science Activation Through Distributed Space Crop Research” led by Principal Investigator Carl Lewis at Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden, Inc. To travel or live in space, humans will need to eat. Growing Beyond Earth trains and equips middle- and high-school classrooms to conduct growth experiments with seeds and crops being evaluated for use as space food. “Sungrazer 2.0: From Armchair Discovery to Data-Driven Comet Science” led by Principal Investigator MaryKay Severino of the ARISA Lab and science lead Karl Battams of the Naval Research Laboratory. The original Sungrazer Project launched in 2006 in response to requests from citizen scientists for verification of comet discoveries. Since then, project volunteers have identified 5,204 comets and counting – the majority of known comets. Sungrazer 2.0 will bring the thrill of comet discovery to new audiences who will join the hunt for comets in images from NASA’s SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory) and STEREO (Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory) missions. “Discovering the SPARC: Space Physics through Amateur Radio Communications” led by Principal Investigator Nathaniel Frissell of the University of Scranton. Since 2017 amateur radio operators have worked together in the Ham Radio Science Citizen Investigation (HamSCI) community to study Earth’s ionosphere through carefully designed and conducted investigations of how their signals bounce off this high, ionized layer of Earth’s atmosphere. This project will bring hands-on space weather science to communities nationwide through amateur radio equipment and enroll high schools in a national research network. “Telescopes for All: Promoting audience engagement with NASA science via participatory data experiences using robotic telescopes” led by Principal Investigator Mary Dussault of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. This project will expand public access to a suite of 22 user-friendly, professional robotic telescopes. This access will allow people to observe, analyze, and contribute to NASA-aligned research, including the search and study of exoplanets and other citizen science projects. “Researchers Inspiring Public Participation in Lake Education and Science (RIPPLES)” led by Principal Investigator Sarah Yelton and science lead Tamlin Pavelsky, both at the University Of North Carolina, Chapel Hill. This project will collaborate with the Lake Observations by Citizen Scientists and Satellites (LOCSS) project to expand participation in lake and reservoir level monitoring. Submitted data will be used to validate observations such as those made by NASA’s SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography) mission. “ARK (Antarctic Resilience and Knowledge): A Collaborative Network for Discovery and Education of Antarctica’s Iconic Species and their Changing Habitats” led by Principal Investigator Sharon Stammerjohn at the University of Colorado, Boulder. This project will invite you to examine NASA’s very high-resolution satellite images of Antarctica to study and monitor habitat changes affecting penguin, seal, and whale populations. With validation by scientists and integration of machine-assisted detection tools, this project will expand the analytical capacity of Antarctic researchers and build public literacy in polar ecosystem science. “Arctic Learning and Engagement with NASA Data for Community Solutions (Arctic LENS)” led by Principal Investigator Katie Spellman of the University of Alaska Fairbanks. This project will invite Alaskans to contribute seasonal environmental monitoring (snow, ice, aurora, spring ice-out, and green-up) in support of NASA missions including FORTE (Arctic Coastlines: Frontlines of Rapidly Transforming Ecosystems), SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography), PACE (Phytoplankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem), and Landsat. El astronauta emérito y capitán retirado de la Marina de los EE. UU. comienza su nuevo rol en el centro de excelencia de la NASA para la robótica y la exploración del espacio profundo y en Caltech, que gestiona JPL para la NASA, el […]
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Caltech nombra al comandante de Artemis II, Reid Wiseman, como subdirector de NASA JPL**

Reid Wiseman, el comandante de la misión Artemis II, ha sido nombrado como el nuevo subdirector del Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) de la NASA y vicepresidente asociado de Caltech. Su incorporación a estas instituciones de prestigio comenzará el 30 de noviembre de 2026. Wiseman, un astronauta emérito y capitán retirado de la Marina de los EE. UU., ha tenido una carrera destacada en la exploración espacial, incluyendo un histórico vuelo lunar que lo llevó a recorrer 695,081 millas, la mayor distancia jamás alcanzada por humanos.

El administrador de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, destacó la experiencia y el liderazgo de Wiseman, afirmando que su trayectoria en misiones de alta complejidad lo convierte en un activo valioso para el JPL. Durante su tiempo en la NASA, Wiseman ha liderado la seguridad de vuelos tripulados y ha participado en numerosas investigaciones científicas.

En su nuevo rol, será responsable de la dirección estratégica y la mejora continua de las operaciones del laboratorio, además de actuar como el principal enlace para programas de seguridad nacional. Este nombramiento se produce en un momento crucial, ya que el JPL se prepara para celebrar su 90 aniversario, consolidando su legado en la exploración espacial.
article.original_title: Caltech Names Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman as NASA JPL Deputy
article.source_body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Former NASA astronaut and Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman joins Caltech and NASA JPL as Caltech associate vice president and JPL deputy director on Nov. 30. Photo Credit: NASA Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on Nov. 30, 2026. “Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “As commander of Artemis II, he helped carry America back around the Moon, and now, as an emeritus astronaut, he will continue giving back to NASA from a new vantage point at JPL. Reid is joining a storied laboratory that has made an enormous amount of history, and there is a lot more ahead. I am excited to see what he and the JPL team accomplish in the years to come.” During the Artemis II test flight, Wiseman , Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen journeyed 695,081 miles on a lunar flyby that took them farther than any humans have ever traveled before. “It feels fitting for Reid, who with the Artemis II crew traveled farther from Earth than any human in history, to join Caltech and JPL — institutions that for nearly 90 years have sent spacecraft into the far reaches of our solar system and beyond,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director and Caltech vice president. “Reid shares our drive for discovery, knows what it takes to lead teams through high-stakes missions, and has a remarkable ability to inspire people everywhere. He adds incredible bench strength to our leadership team as we build on the lab’s legacy and shape its future together.” After joining NASA’s astronaut corps in 2009, Wiseman went on to serve as flight engineer aboard the International Space Station for the 165-day Expedition 41 mission in 2014 and was a commander of NASA’s 21st Extreme Environment Mission Operations expedition, during which he lived for eight days in a habitat on the ocean floor in 2016. As the agency’s chief astronaut from December 2020 to November 2022, Wiseman led NASA’s astronaut corps, overseeing crew flight readiness and crew safety for all NASA human spaceflight missions. During his years of service at the agency, he has conducted hundreds of scientific experiments. “I’ve explored the furthest reaches of what a human can explore at NASA — and there were truly no words in the English vocabulary to describe seeing the Sun disappear behind the Moon from deep space. But that experience was really the jumping off point to go do the impossible things that Caltech and JPL dream, dare together, and do for NASA and the nation,” Wiseman said. “What an awesome time in my career to join this team and to try and push humanity and push our understanding of the solar system and the universe.” Wiseman joins JPL, NASA’s only federally funded research and development center, as the lab approaches its 90th anniversary since being founded by Caltech. In his role as Caltech’s associate vice president and JPL deputy director, Wiseman will be responsible for the strategic leadership, stewardship and continuous improvement of laboratory operations, including close partnership with Caltech on institutional planning, management and compliance. Serving as Center Management Authority for JPL mission execution, Wiseman will ensure operational excellence across mission support functions in accordance with NASA requirements and applicable federal and state regulations. In addition, he will be JPL’s primary interface for national security programs. “Reid brings to Caltech and JPL a truly unprecedented view of what humanity can achieve when ingenuity and determination are matched with the courage to pursue the furthest frontiers,” said Caltech president Ray Jayawardhana. “His pioneering spirit coupled with unbounded curiosity make him a natural fit for Caltech and JPL, a force-multiplier for a community whose daring continues to push the limits of humanity’s reach. I look forward to working closely with Dave and Reid as we chart our next era of exploration in partnership with NASA, elevating America’s space ambitions to breathtaking new heights.” After receiving a bachelor’s degree in computer and systems engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Wiseman joined the Navy, going on to fly combat missions and serve as a test pilot. He also has a master’s degree in systems engineering from Johns Hopkins University in his hometown of Baltimore. -end- Media Contact Matthew Segal Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif. 818-354-8307 matthew.j.segal@jpl.nasa.gov 2026-077 Share Details Last Updated Oct 28, 2026 Related Terms Jet Propulsion Laboratory Artemis 2 Explore More 6 min read NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust Article 3 days ago 5 min read NASA JPL Looks to Next 90 Years of Innovation, Exploration Article 1 week ago 6 min read NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system… Article 2 weeks ago Keep Exploring Discover Related Topics Artemis II Jet Propulsion Laboratory Robotics Earth’s Moon The Moon makes Earth more livable, sets the rhythm of ocean tides, and keeps a record of our solar system’s…

article.description: Sismo en Venezuela: Estudio de la Universidad de Chile revela cómo se movió el suelo durante el terremoto en La Guaira Megatiempo
article.explanation:
Un reciente estudio realizado por la Universidad de Chile ha analizado el movimiento del suelo durante el terremoto que afectó a La Guaira, Venezuela. Este tipo de investigaciones son fundamentales para entender cómo se comporta el terreno durante eventos sísmicos, lo que puede ayudar en la preparación y mitigación de desastres en el futuro.

El estudio se centra en los patrones de movimiento del suelo, lo que permite a los científicos identificar las características específicas del sismo y su impacto en la región. Comprender estos movimientos es crucial para mejorar las construcciones y la infraestructura en áreas propensas a terremotos, así como para desarrollar mejores modelos de predicción y respuesta ante futuros eventos sísmicos. 

Este tipo de investigaciones no solo aporta al conocimiento científico, sino que también tiene implicaciones prácticas para la seguridad de las comunidades afectadas por sismos.

article.description: Frente a la costa de la Isla de Vancouver, una placa oceánica se está desintegrando, brindando a los científicos su primera visión clara de una zona de subducción en proceso de muerte. Futura, el medio que explora el mundo.
article.explanation:
Frente a la costa de la Isla de Vancouver, se ha observado que una placa oceánica está en proceso de desintegración. Este fenómeno ha permitido a los científicos obtener una visión más clara de una zona de subducción que se encuentra en un estado de deterioro. Las zonas de subducción son áreas donde una placa tectónica se desliza por debajo de otra, y su estudio es crucial para entender los procesos geológicos que ocurren en el fondo marino.

La desintegración de esta placa oceánica ofrece una oportunidad única para investigar cómo estas zonas pueden cambiar con el tiempo y qué implica su "muerte" en términos geológicos. Este tipo de investigación es fundamental para ampliar nuestro conocimiento sobre la dinámica de la Tierra y los procesos que afectan la formación y destrucción de las placas tectónicas.

Esta ampliación del estudio refleja el interés de la empresa en explorar más a fondo el potencial mineral de la zona, que es conocida por su riqueza en recursos naturales.

El estudio geofísico es una herramienta clave en la minería, ya que permite a las empresas obtener información sobre la composición del subsuelo sin necesidad de realizar excavaciones extensivas. Al ampliar este estudio, Blade Resources busca mejorar su comprensión de la geología local y localizar áreas que podrían ser económicamente viables para la extracción de metales preciosos.

Este movimiento se enmarca dentro de una tendencia más amplia en la industria minera, donde las empresas están invirtiendo en tecnología y estudios geofísicos para optimizar sus operaciones y maximizar la eficiencia en la búsqueda de recursos.

article.description: La primera tormenta nombrada de la temporada de ciclones del océano Índico norte tocó tierra a lo largo de la costa de Andhra Pradesh.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Ciclón Arnab Devasta la Costa Este de India**

El ciclón Arnab, la primera tormenta nombrada de la temporada de ciclones del Océano Índico Norte 2026, se formó en la Bahía de Bengala el 25 de octubre. Con vientos sostenidos de hasta 140 kilómetros por hora, el fenómeno meteorológico tocó tierra en la costa de Andhra Pradesh y Yanam el 28 de octubre, donde se registraron vientos de 130 kilómetros por hora, clasificándose como un "ciclón muy severo" según el Departamento Meteorológico de India (IMD).

La tormenta impactó entre Bapatla y Visakhapatnam, una región densamente poblada que alberga grandes ciudades y comunidades pesqueras. Arnab causó daños extensos, derribando árboles, inundando cultivos y hogares, y afectando las operaciones pesqueras y las redes de transporte y energía. Las autoridades indias evacuaron a más de 84,000 personas de áreas costeras vulnerables antes de la llegada del ciclón.

Este evento se produce en el contexto de un fenómeno de El Niño, que altera las condiciones oceánicas y puede influir en la actividad ciclónica. A pesar de que se espera una reducción en la frecuencia e intensidad de los ciclones durante años de El Niño, Arnab ha demostrado ser una excepción significativa, dejando a su paso un saldo de al menos tres víctimas fatales y una devastación considerable en la región.
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Arnab Strikes India Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search The first named storm of the 2026 North Indian Ocean cyclone season—Arnab (pronounced Or-nab)—emerged in the Bay of Bengal on October 25, a rather late start for a basin that typically produces named cyclones in April or May. When the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on NOAA-20 captured this nighttime image at 20:12 Universal Time on October 26 (1:42 a.m. India Standard Time on October 27), the storm had sustained winds of about 140 kilometers (85 miles) per hour, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). When Arnab made landfall on the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coast early on October 28, sustained winds were 130 kilometers per hour. IMD categorizes a storm that strength as a “very severe cyclonic storm ,” which is similar to a Category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale . It made landfall between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, a heavily settled area home to large cities, farmland, and fishing communities. Arnab caused extensive damage, uprooting trees, inundating crops and homes, limiting fishing operations, and disrupting transportation and power networks, according to news reports . Prior to landfall, Indian authorities had evacuated tens of thousands of people from vulnerable coastal areas. The storm comes in the midst of an El Niño , a climate pattern marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific that emerges roughly every two to seven years. The changed ocean conditions can influence the atmosphere in ways that alter global weather patterns and change the distribution of rainfall, winds, tropical cyclones, fires, floods, and other phenomena. In the Bay of Bengal, for instance, some research indicates that altered environmental conditions during an El Niño are associated with a reduction in tropical cyclone activity. The ocean basin sees both less frequent and less intense tropical cyclones during El Niño years, researchers have found. article.description: Cuando las empresas comenzaron a acercarse al Centro de Investigación Langley de la NASA, pidiendo ser incluidas en el Estado de Juego de Servicios, Ensamblaje y Fabricación en el Espacio (ISAM) para acceder a inteligencia competitiva, el equipo supo que habían cruzado un punto de inflexión. “Hemos tenido algunas empresas no nombradas que preguntan si tenemos alguna información confidencial”, dice Dale Arney, líder senior del equipo […]
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Estado Actual del ISAM de la NASA: El Estándar de la Industria para el Servicio, Ensamblaje y Fabricación en el Espacio**

El In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing (ISAM) de la NASA ha alcanzado un hito significativo en su desarrollo, según el último informe publicado en octubre de 2026. Este documento, que abarca 368 páginas, detalla las capacidades actuales de ISAM en 11 áreas funcionales, incluyendo manipulación robótica y reabastecimiento, y se ha convertido en un recurso esencial para la industria espacial.

Desde su lanzamiento en 2021, el ISAM State of Play ha evolucionado, reflejando un crecimiento exponencial en el campo. Dale Arney, líder del equipo de tecnología ISAM en el Centro de Investigación Langley de la NASA, destacó que el documento no solo sirve como una enciclopedia, sino también como una hoja de ruta para las tecnologías que permitirán el servicio y ensamblaje de naves espaciales en órbita.

El informe se basa en criterios estrictos de entrada, asegurando que solo se incluyan tecnologías que existan físicamente, ya sea como prototipos en tierra o demostraciones en vuelo. Esto garantiza que el ISAM State of Play sea un recurso confiable para empresas que buscan entender y participar en este ecosistema en expansión.

Con la mirada puesta en misiones futuras más ambiciosas, el ISAM State of Play se posiciona como un documento clave que proporciona un vocabulario compartido y una base de capacidades necesarias para el desarrollo de infraestructuras lunares y manufactura en órbita.
article.original_title: NASA’s ISAM State of Play: The Industry Standard for Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing
article.source_body: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) When companies began approaching NASA’s Langley Research Center, asking to be included in the In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing (ISAM) State of Play for access to competitive intelligence, the team knew they had crossed an inflection point. “We’ve had some unnamed companies ask if we have any proprietary information,” says Dale Arney, senior team lead for the ISAM Technology Portfolio at NASA Langley. The answer is “no,” but that impartiality is precisely what makes the State of Play invaluable to an industry trying to understand a rapidly expanding field. The cover of the ISAM State of Play, featuring Astronaut F. Story Musgrave, anchored on the Space Shuttle Endeavor’s robotic arm, preparing to be elevated to the top of the Hubble Space Telescope during Hubble’s first servicing mission in 1993. Credit: NASA Published since 2021, the 2026 edition has grown to 368 pages documenting current ISAM capabilities across 11 functional areas, from robotic manipulation to refueling and structural assembly. The document serves as both encyclopedia and roadmap for the technologies that will enable spacecraft to be serviced, assembled, and manufactured in orbit rather than launched as integrated systems. “The field itself has expanded more than linearly since we started,” Arney explains. What began as a tool to ensure NASA centers shared a common reference point has become the industry’s go-to resource for understanding what’s possible versus what’s still conceptual. The State of Play team maintains strict entry criteria: hardware must physically exist, either as ground prototypes or in-flight demonstrations. “We get people who will send their PowerPoint presentation of their technology idea,” Arney notes. “There’s no real indication they’ve done any work on the technology itself yet.” Those concepts don’t make the cut until the following year’s review. This rigor matters, because ISAM capabilities will enable missions impossible with traditional single-launch approaches. Future missions will require telescopes larger than any launch vehicle fairing, persistent national security assets that are mobile and resilient, and commercial systems that can upgrade to the latest technology on orbit without full replacement. The document is intentionally collaborative. “We like to refer to it as kind of a crowdsource document,” says team member John Mulvaney. Each year brings more interviews with industry partners to ensure accuracy and completeness. Contributions come from NASA centers including Ames, Glenn, Marshall, Kennedy, and Johnson, along with international developers meeting the hardware criteria. The result is more than a technical reference. The 2026 edition includes developer profiles and facilities documentation, providing mission designers with not just what’s possible but who’s doing it and where the work happens. For companies entering the ISAM ecosystem or expanding their capabilities, it offers both competitive context and collaboration opportunities. As the space industry moves toward more ambitious missions, from lunar infrastructure to on-orbit manufacturing, the ISAM State of Play provides the shared vocabulary and capability baseline that emerging ecosystems require. It’s not speculation about the future; it’s documentation of what exists now and where the hardware is heading next. **TITULAR: La Tierra de las Rocas de Pie**

**CATEGORÍA: volcanes**

Un nuevo estudio geológico ha revelado la fascinante historia del Parque Nacional Chiricahua, ubicado en el sureste de Arizona, Estados Unidos. Hace aproximadamente 27 millones de años, un volcán en esta región provocó una serie de erupciones explosivas que dispersaron más de 1,000 veces la cantidad de material volcánico que el Monte St. Helens en 1980. Este evento dejó una huella geológica significativa, creando la caldera de Turkey Creek, que mide aproximadamente 19 kilómetros de ancho y 1,500 metros de profundidad.

Las erupciones generaron flujos piroclásticos que se solidificaron en depósitos de toba riolítica, formando impresionantes formaciones rocosas que hoy se conocen como "las rocas de pie". La erosión y el desgaste han esculpido este paisaje en un laberinto de pináculos y cañones, convirtiéndolo en un destino turístico popular.

Designado como monumento nacional en 1924 y posteriormente como Parque Nacional en octubre de 2026, Chiricahua alberga una rica biodiversidad, con más de 1,000 especies de plantas que prosperan en sus diversos ecosistemas. Este parque no solo preserva su geología única, sino que también se ha convertido en un refugio para la flora y fauna de la región.
article.original_title: The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Some 27 million years ago, a volcano in what’s now southeastern Arizona unleashed a spectacular series of eruptions, strewing more than 1,000 times as much volcanic material across the landscape as Mount St. Helens did in 1980. The explosive eruptions blanketed the region, part of the Chiricahua Apache Nation’s traditional lands, with ash and pumice . Layered into this were massive pyroclastic flows that hardened into deposits of welded rhyolitic tuff that in some areas were nearly 1,600 feet (500 meters) thick, about three times the height of the Washington Monument. As the magma chamber emptied, the ground above it collapsed, leaving a gaping depression—the Turkey Creek caldera —that was roughly 12 miles (19 kilometers) wide and 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) deep. An array of geologic processes, including erosion and weathering , gradually sculpted the welded layer of tuff into the collection of dramatic spires, hoodoos , and canyons that visitors to the caldera area encounter today. The Apache called the area “ The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks ” for good reason. Hiking through Rhyolite Canyon or driving through Bonita Canyon means encountering a dizzying maze of rock pinnacles, some hundreds of feet tall. Others, like Big Balanced Rock , have surprisingly large boulders precariously perched on top. Meanwhile, those at Heart of Rocks and Massai Point are gathered into groups of hundreds. The area was designated a national monument in 1924 to preserve its remarkable geology. In October 2026, it was redesignated as Chiricahua National Park (pronounced cheery-cow-ah ). The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this cloud-free image of the new national park on July 2, 2026. Individual rock spires are too small to distinguish, but the eroding rhyolitic tuff landscape appears gray. Stream valleys dense with trees and other vegetation, including Rhyolite Canyon and Bonita Canyon, snake across the landscape. With four biogeographic regions converging in the park—the Sonoran Desert, the Chihuahuan Desert, the Rocky Mountains, and the Sierra Madre—it is a haven of plant diversity . Among the 1,000 species growing within the park’s varied desert, grassland, chaparral, deciduous forest, and coniferous forest ecosystems are agaves, prickly pear cacti, yuccas, manzanita, pine, fir, cypress, sycamore, juniper, and oak. The park’s location within the Chiricahua Mountains puts it among several “ sky islands ” in Arizona—isolated mountain ranges that emerge from the surrounding desert “sea.” According to the National Park Service , the range’s highest point (outside the park) rises 2,986 meters (9,795 feet) above sea level, more than 1,800 meters above the surrounding valley. NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Adam Voiland.
